utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Ms. Chittenden, for the Prosecution, has some questions for you. Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please, could you state your name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And what qualifications do you have in this field?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I have a basic medical qualification of Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery. I'm a -- a pathology qualification, which is the Fellow of the Oncology Pathologists in the UK, and I have a forensic qualification, a Diploma of Forensic Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And for how long have you been a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: About 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, do you recall testifying in the trials of Prosecutor and Krstic in May 2000 and Prosecutor and Popovic in February 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your testimony at that time truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to review that testimony before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to offer into evidence the witness's testimony in the Krstic and Popovic trials as Exhibits P897 and P892, respectively. I would also like to offer into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. The two exhibits, P892 and P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- 897 will be received with these exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to offer into evidence the exhibits admitted through this witness in the Popovic trial. They are Exhibits P893, P895, and P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's enough if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: It's enough? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- mention the last number of the whole set of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And P897 through P918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They all will be received, but one doesn't have a translation. This is 898, yes, and this will only be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to offer into evidence this witness's three expert reports as chief pathologist for the 1999, 2000, and 2001 exhumation seasons in Bosnia which were admitted via him in Popovic, and they are Exhibits P894, P896, and P919.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just received the whole list, starting with P893 through P919, and, therefore, they are included in that set.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I now have a short summary to read, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I'm going to read out a short summary of your testimony in the Popovic trial, and after that I'll have a few questions for you before you're cross-examined. Dr. Clark testified before this Tribunal regarding the Srebrenica-related grave-sites during the trial of Radislav Krstic on 30 and 31 May 2000 and during the trial of Vujadin Popovic et al on 19 and 20 February 2007. Dr. Clark is a forensic pathologist based in Glasgow in the United Kingdom. In 1999, 2000 and 2001, he worked for the Office of the Prosecutor as the chief pathologist for mortuary operations for the Bosnia exhumations. Prior to this, Dr. Clark volunteered for several days in 1998 as a forensic pathologist for the OTP exhumations that season. Dr. Clark performed autopsies of victims recovered from mass graves associated with the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. Dr. Clark's role was to look at the bodies which had been taken from the grave-sites by the field team, to identify injuries on the bodies, and to try to establish cause of death. The pathologists also assisted with identification and retrieval of any other evidence on the bodies. In addition, as chief pathologist, Dr. Clark was responsible for overseeing the staff and workings of the mortuary, including the anthropologists and support staff, of scene-of-crime officers, photographer, radiographer, and secretaries. In 1999, Dr. Clark produced a report summarising the results of the 1999 post-mortem examinations of the bodies recovered from the primary grave-sites of Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova. In 2000, he produced a report summarising the reports of that season's post-mortem examinations recovered from Lazete, Glogova and Ravnice. In 2001, he produced a report summarising the results of that season's exhumations and examinations from Ravnice, Glogova and Zeleni Jadar. In the post-mortem examinations that Dr. Clark performed in 1999, 2000 and 2001, he found that nearly all of the bodies in the grave-sites were men, ranging in age, with many of them being young. None of the men found in the grave-sites were wearing military uniforms or had weapons in their possession. Dr. Clark found that the majority of victims were killed by high-velocity gun-shot wounds. And as much as could be determined, most of them had been shot from behind. Dr. Clark also made specific findings in relation to each of the graves. In relation to the primary grave-site of Glogova, he testified that some of the bodies exhibited gun-shot and blast injuries, in keeping with the allegations relating to the Kravica warehouse execution -- sorry, incident. Similar gun-shot and blast injuries were also found on the bodies recovered from the secondary grave-site of Zeleni Jadar. Also in this general Glogova grave-site was a separate grave containing the remains of 12 men who had been tied together in pairs and shot in the back or the side of the head, probably at close range. Dr. Clark also reported that some of the victims at Kozluk, Lazete, Nova Kasaba, and Glogova were found with hand ligatures and/or blindfolds. Finally, at the Ravnice primary grave-site he found the bodies were not buried, but lying largely on the surface, and thus greatly broken up and scattered. None were blindfolded. The injuries were all gun-shot, mostly multiple, but there were no blast injuries. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. I now have a few questions to ask Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I would like to mention that in your first tendering move, you were not mentioning P919, the report of the witness, but that was included in the decision of the Chamber, to receive that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, that was my omission. Yes, I would like to include that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's clear for the record now. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, what was your role as a pathologist in the Bosnia exhumations in 1999 through 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, as a pathologist, I was one of a number of pathologists doing what pathologists do. That's to examine bodies, record our findings in them, and secure any evidence from them. The main findings were interpretation of the injuries on the body. So that was our primary role, to look at the bodies, see what findings there were, particularly describe the injuries, and then try and establish or provide a cause of death. And then, myself, I had a further role as chief pathologist, as you described the various duties I had for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And what were those specific tasks as chief pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, that was, as you've said, to make sure that the -- or oversee the general running of the mortuary, the staffing, that we had enough people, the -- I organised the sort of flow of work so that -- the pace of work and the cases that we did. I acted as -- I offered advice to colleagues and any others, and to just generally make sure that the place worked well and efficiently. And as you said, probably my major task was -- after all the practical work had been finished, was to look through all the post-mortem reports and try and extract the relevant information from them, and bring them to some coherent whole, which is what these reports that are the overall reports I've produced are.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Clark, in your reports and in your prior testimony, you explained the procedure at the mortuary when the bodies were brought to be examined after being transferred from the grave-sites. With the assistance of some photographs, I'd like you to briefly explain that procedure to us now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 6593 in e-court, please. If we can go to page 2 firstly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you tell us about what's happening in this photo here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure how clear it is. This is a very general view of the mortuary, a sort of random -- random picture of the mortuary. I think that's maybe slightly better there. You'll see various people in it. Essentially, we've got a number of processes. Right at the back, you'll see people in blue and white, et cetera. They are the people who are actually examining the bodies. The bodies have been taken out of fridges, they've been put onto tables. The bodies are cleaned up, kind of reorganised, because a lot of them were skeletons, and the clothing removed and any other possessions, so that's what's going on there. And we will -- the pathologists, in turn, will be noting -- noting the various findings. The person in the middle of the photograph, sitting with the dark blue and with the gloves on, is a photographer, and it's his job to be recording all the relevant evidence as things were going on. So he does that, and then he comes and files his pictures. And the person at the bottom right is, who -- you just see the light blue. He's a scene-of-crime officer, and it's his job to -- if we find any possessions or anything else on the body, to take hold of these and record them and make sure that they are -- the chain of evidence. So that's the general working. Just to go back to the people at the back there --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you, there's a close-up photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can just go to page 1 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is now a close-up of the sort of working area. There are three tables, if you like, three teams, going on. At the back there, we have a body. You can see the dark-brown material there. That's a body with clothing and with sort of mud from the grave. That's actually myself working at the right-hand side there. I'm assisted with -- by an anthropologist, a technician, and various other people, so we're all working together. We all have little specific jobs to do. So that's actually what's going on there. And there are three similar teams working in the mortuary doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can just turn to the final page, number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is kind of slightly further on. This is a body -- a skeletonised body laid out on a table. We've cleaned it, we've removed the clothing. We've reorganised the bones with the help of the anthropologists, and now we're doing -- recording our findings. This person in the front here happens to be an anthropologist who is noting the bones which are present and trying to assess the age of the person and the sex of the person. The role of the pathologist is also to look at the body, but really from the point of view of looking for injuries and identifying where they are, what caused them, and things like that. And you can see the various processes going on in the background. Generally, perhaps in a day, we would do, on a case like this, perhaps 12, 15 bodies per day going through the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. We're finished with that photo now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you just mentioned before pathologists and anthropologists working together at the mortuary. Can you explain the difference, just once again, between their work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. A pathologist is medically trained, so we deal with people, we deal with the whole body. Anthropologists are not medically trained, but they have a specific expertise in looking at the skeleton, the bones. Their role in the mortuary here was really twofold. Firstly, to look at the bones, because it's really mainly from the bones that you can tell the age of the person and the sex of the person in cases like this. So they would be looking for that, the shape of the skull, the shape of the pelvis, things like that. They would also make an inventory of all the bones which were present, because some would be missing. They would list that. But because of their knowledge -- detailed knowledge of the shape of bones, where we had a broken bone, maybe in several pieces, they had that skill to be able to identify that little fragment came from that bone or whatever and perhaps glue them all together, and that made any injuries, bullet injuries particularly, all the more easy to see. So they had that dual role of assisting with identification, but also assisting the pathologists to clarify the injuries. Now, it's one thing finding an injury. It's another thing interpreting what that means, and that really is where the pathologist comes in, because with our knowledge of the rest of the body, all the soft tissues and the organs, we can get a very good idea that an injury to a bone is likely to cause these other -- the damage elsewhere in the body. So that was why the pathologist has the ultimate responsibility of the consequences of an injury and of establishing why we thought how this person would have died. So there's kind of two roles there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to just show you now P895 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden, are you tendering the three photographs we have seen?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to tender this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The three coloured photographs, Your Honours, under 65 ter 06593 will be assigned P01127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have Exhibit P895, and if we could first go to page 4. Now, this report doesn't have a B/C/S translation -- oh, maybe it does. Okay, great. Okay, if we can go to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. The -- on the right-hand side -- I suppose it's on both sides. This is our working document in the mortuary. We had -- it's about 12 pages or so. And so this is what we would have on a clip board, as we're looking at the body, taking notes. And you can see lots of scoring out there, et cetera, because, you know, we're thinking about things, changing our minds, perhaps. So this is our rough notes taken at the time. And we go through various stages. This is -- right on the first page here -- well, in addition to the official details of each case and who's involved, on the first page is just a very general overview of the body, its state and things like that. And then as you go through the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please, in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we go through and we then begin to detail the clothing in a little more detail. It has to be said, just specifically, on that part of clothing, that was usually filled up after the clothing had been cleaned. We came back and filled that in afterwards. But what we're looking for in the clothing is perhaps signs of bullet injuries, any burning, anything else or any other damage that we might find on it. Then we look at the sort of -- I'll put my specs on for this, I think. These other items at the bottom of the page here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Just the bottom half, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are perhaps material which has been taken out of the body. In the pockets, cigarette lighters or what have you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This page is really about general identification features. A lot of it, we cannot tell, but if we could tell just looking from the body whether this was male or female, because sometimes the body was complete, we could indicate that. More often than not, as a pathologist, we weren't able to say. We're looking at the general build, any hair that's present, teeth, things like that, just the general identification features.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And the next page, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a page actually specifically compiled by the anthropologists, so I can't really speak too much about that. But this is -- they are looking at the pelvis and the skull to try and get an idea of the sex of this person, the height, and a rough idea of the age. They compile that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, again, that's -- anthropologists complete this. It's a sort of inventory for the body. You know, take for the head, it's present, the left arm, right arm, whether it's present or not. Really, in this body, it's more or less intact. I think you can see all the ticks are in the "Present."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, this is our main role. This is looking at the injuries. Before we do anything on the bodies, we took the body into a special room and did a fluoroscope on it. This is a form of X-ray which really just scans the whole body and will pick up any metal fragments, particularly bullets. And we would do that for every body and see if we could identify these. After that -- yes. Then we go down to systematically look at injuries on the different parts of the body. You can see that the sort of lower half of the thing is about head and neck. I'm looking for injuries in the head and neck. You'll see nothing written there, so there's no injuries on the head and neck. If you go on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- then you will see that we are now moving on to the trunk and that I have now started to describe. I have findings on the trunk, and I've numbered them and described it in some detail. I've then got to decide -- I'm given three options: whether I think this is an injury which is caused in life; whether I think it's probably an injury caused after death; or whether I really don't know. Now, we can come on to later on decide why we think injuries are caused in life or not, but it's probably easier to do that later. But you'll see that that first injury, this is an injury in the upper part of the chest here in which there's a big hole in the skin because this body [indiscernible], and there were fragments of -- there was disruption of the ribcage -- there was a big hole in the ribcage underneath that, and I found fragments of bullet. So I was happy that this represented a gun-shot injury on the chest. I also find, under number 2 here, sorry, multiple broken ribs. This was a pattern that we saw in a lot of bodies, and we give the benefit of the doubt that these were probably injuries caused after death, just as the body is pressing in the grave and compacted by other ones. So you'll see the tick, I think, if you go to the right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: On the screen, if we can just -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I've put "Probably post-mortem."

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. So the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you just go down to the bottom of that page, I think it's probably empty, but -- yes, it is. So the next page. So really that was the only injury on the body. We looked at -- if there was any internal -- internal tissues. This was unusual, that it was a relatively complete body. We can actually see internal organs, and I didn't find -- I was looking for any natural disease in these and I found none.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next, I have recorded what photographs were taken of the body, in general terms, and the name of the photographer doing it. I've recorded what samples were taken from the body. This would be any samples of bullet, samples taken for the anthropologist to try and assess further the age of the person, samples for DNA, for attempts at future identification. So these are all recorded in that report there and given numbers; C1, C2, D1, D2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This doesn't look very well. Scored out as well. This is my -- from the -- from my workings from my findings, I've now formulated conclusions. This is done usually after, you know, maybe in the days afterwards. We don't do that at the time because we need to sit down and think about things. So it's not just rushed off at the end of each case. It is considered. And I give a summary of my findings. It was an intact body. We established the person was male, about the clothing, et cetera. And I've said there was evidence of an apparent gun-shot injury to the right side of the chest, with damage to the ribcage and the rest of it. And I've concluded that was a potentially fatal injury. I've noted the other injuries which were present, the fractured ribs which I thought were post-mortem in nature, and I finally at the end there come to give a cause of death. I thought the cause of death was a gun-shot wound of the chest. And I've signed it and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And just the final page, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a body diagram, and I'm just -- the dark area on the chest is just the area of disruption of this --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So if we could just now go back to -- we started from page 4 on, for the record. If we could go back to page 1 of this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And if you could just briefly tell us, what's this here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: From all these rough notes and scribbles and scores-out, that folder is given to the secretaries, and they bring that all together into a nice, tight, three-page report, with my conclusions at the front there, the cause of death, and then the details which we've heard about summarised on the next two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is just simply a typed version of the rough notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I've finished with that exhibit now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you've mentioned bodies and body parts. Can you explain how something is classified as a body versus a body part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it was quite common, and particularly in some graves, that we found intact bodies, but we also found large numbers of just a little bit of a body, perhaps an arm, perhaps a hand, a couple of ribs, sometimes slightly bigger, and we just called them body parts. They were part of a body. I mean, it's easy if you've just got a hand or a bit of skull. It's a part of a body in everybody's language. When it became a bit bigger, perhaps with the head and the trunk, most of the trunk, but no arms, no legs, is that a body part or a body? We took the view that anything which was substantially a body, in fact, there was more of a body or not, we called a body. So generally that would be some -- if there was a head there and the trunk, I would call that a body because it was -- it's a person, really, and it's identifiable. If it was just a leg or two legs, I would call that a body part. Now, there was a decision taken at the field team - I think you've heard Professor Wright testify here - and they would give a initial assessment. They would call it a body or a body part. By the time it came to the mortuary -- or after the mortuary, rather, when we'd had the chance to clean up the bodies and perhaps find extra bits there, we sometimes changed their allocation from -- of a body down to a body part or the other way 'round, a body part up to a body, and that was quite acceptable and not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And were autopsy reports prepared for both body parts as well as bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And in your final pathology reports for 1999, 2000 and 2001, did you include those results for the body parts in your final calculations about cause of death and gun-shot injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I mean, I've discussed body parts, but I've kind of left them to the side, and my main -- or the calculations about how -- the types of injuries, how common they are, the directions, et cetera, are entirely based on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: So we're not confusing ourselves with body parts. The problem is, of all these body parts, I don't know if some of them came from the main bodies where a bit's missing, or did they come from other bodies who we haven't yet found, and we did not have the ability or the facilities to -- or the time to match all these up. So it was easy just to record what was there, but dismiss them from the overall calculations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I've just got a few more -- a couple more questions to ask you and then a few photos, and then we'll be finished. In your Popovic testimony and also in all of your three reports, you explain the limitations of pathology evidence in these cases. Can you briefly outline those for us now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is a very important concept to get over. These were not cases which -- the type of cases a forensic pathologist normally deals with. We normally deal with people who are freshly dead, who have all the tissues on them, you can recognise colours and injuries and any other findings. So we're not really dealing with the normal situation. We're dealing with decomposed bodies, often very discoloured just because of soil and other staining. Lots of the tissues will be missing and very often -- very often with no tissues left, just skeletons. And we've got to try and assess our findings in that. There's really four stages. When we look at the body -- these decomposed bodies, and we see something, we've got to decide is that genuine or is it not? Is this just staining which has occurred in the grave-site from a body nearby, discolouration, or some odd mark on the bone? We've got to decide that. Having decided that I think this is an injury, a genuine injury, the second stage is to decide did that injury occur before death or after death, because we've got to be very well aware of the possibility of injuries occurring to the bodies after death, and that could occur for a number of reasons. Bodies have been put into a mass grave, they're perhaps crushed together or lying heavily on top of each other. You can imagine pressure on the chest or the pelvis, and these bones can break. Bodies have also been removed from one grave to another, potentially, disrupted. So there's quite a potential for injuries to occur to the bodies after death. So we've got to decide whether this has occurred before death or after death. So the third stage, having decided I think this is an injury which has occurred in life, I've got to decide what kind of injury is it. Is this an injury caused by being hit by some weapon, by a gun-shot, by a knife, by falling? And really we're talking about injuries on the bones here, because most of the bodies were skeletonised. So that was a further assessment, had to do that. And the fourth stage was, having decided this is a genuine injury, having decided this is probably gun-shot injury, I've then got to decide did that kill them, because you may have a gun-shot injury through your hand and that's not necessarily going to kill you, or an injury through your forearm won't necessarily kill you. So I've got to decide whether -- whether that's likely to be a fatal injury. And as my training as a pathologist, I know what tissues are 'round about the bones and how people normally die because we deal with death all the time, and I could assume that -- I think if I find a bullet hole in the front of the skull and an exit hole at the back, I can be fairly certain that's going to kill that person, even though I can't see the brain in between, but I know it will be there. And, similarly, an injury to the front of the chest, there's a lot of big organs inside the chest which will get damaged. So that was why we could come -- we could come to decide about a cause of death. I have to say we did not come to that lightly, and I think you'll see from the reports that in a substantial number of cases we felt that there wasn't the evidence there to come to a positive cause of death, and these are cases which we left as unascertained. But I think it's very important to get an idea of the difficulties of looking at these bodies and the thoughts we had to have in our mind all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. Considering those limitations, just in general, what was the finding that you found in the majority for cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, it was gun-shot injuries. I think it's -- I've worked out to about -- of these bodies, about 86 per cent of the bodies in these -- all these grave-sites had been -- had gun-shot injuries which we thought were the cause of death. Now, that leaves 14 per cent in which we couldn't find -- well, actually, there's another percentage will have died from blast injuries from explosions, and you would have to add that to them. I think that's about 5 per cent. And then there's a small proportion, and that must be about 9 per cent, 8 or 9 per cent, in which we could not come to a cause of death, and that was possibly because we couldn't find any injuries or we didn't find any injuries on the parts that were present, or we didn't think these injuries, even though they were present, were sufficient to kill. So we sort of -- I think it's important that we were prepared to accept that there were cases that we could not establish cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. Now, finally, just before we finish, I'd like to show you three photos.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If we could have P912 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us about this photo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it's a bit dark. I don't know what colour it comes in. This is a skull from the side on. The right-hand side of the screen is the front as you face. You can see the teeth at the bottom right, and the left-hand side is obviously the back of the skull. This sort of horseshoe-shaped bone to the right-hand side is your cheekbone, so that's -- you're looking at the skull side on. What this injury particularly shows is a bullet hole in the skull, and that is towards the bottom left of the skull. There's not an actual arrow, but I think you can see a black hole towards the bottom left, a circular black hole. That's a gun-shot entry wound. Now, from that, you'll see various lines going up over the rest of the skull. There's certainly one going up and to the right, and there's another one going to the back, and there's some going down below. These are what happens when particularly a high-velocity bullet hits a skull. It loses a lot of energy, and the skull fragments. You get a hole, but you get these fractures running off in all directions, with a lot of disruption of the skull. So that's what it's showing, a gun-shot injury of the skull.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And just before we go to the next photo, what are those letters and numbers down there on the ruler? What does that mean, generally?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The numbers -- oh, yes, sorry. This is the case number. "KP" is "Konjevic Polje," and it was grave 1 of Konjevic Polje, "KP1," and each body is given a number. This was the number given by the field team, so this is the 15th body. And it's "B," that means it's a body, not a body part. So Konjevic Polje, grave 1, the fifth body, and it's a body rather than a body part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we can go to P901 in e-court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. You said first it is the 15th body, and then we saw that you said "the fifth body."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it might be my eyesight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We saw the number 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 15th, then. Sorry, my eyesight might have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: So, Dr. Clark, what do we see here in this --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is another skull, and this is to show a ligature around the face. The skull is rather discoloured, but I think you can see in the middle part a sort of band of pink material going 'round. It's covering the eye sockets and it's tied at the back. And this was a typical blindfold. And this body is from Kozluk, "KK," the third grave at Kozluk, and it's body number 621, and it's a body. So this is just a good example of a ligature -- a blindfold around the neck -- around the face, rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, if we could have P902 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is showing a pair of hands. So the hands are pointing down the way. And this is showing ligature around the wrists. You can see a binding. I think it's tied in the middle. It's looped around each wrist and there was a knot in the middle. So that's what's now showing. This also sure indicates that the varying degree of preservation of the body. This one has tissue on it, sort of leathery -- dark, leathery tissue, skin, where other ones were -- were just a skeleton. So this is Kozluk 3, body 329.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And for these photos, where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: They were all taken in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Chittenden. Mr. Tolimir, now you may commence your cross-examination and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to the witness and everyone present. May God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Clark, in the Popovic et al case, in answer to the question on the terms of reference within your work, you answered the following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... this had to do with Srebrenica. There were other grave-sites, but I suppose that you want to know about the sites related to Srebrenica." This is my question: Being a pathologist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you please repeat the page and line number. The interpreter didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Page 7335, lines 5 and 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Being a pathologist, in what way did you establish that the grave-sites where you worked, Kozluk, Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, Glogova, Ravnice, and Zeleni Jadar, were linked with Srebrenica? Did you make any inquiries of your own or was this something that you were told? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We made no inquiries -- I made no inquiries of my own. These were -- this was information provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And just for the record, we are looking at document P892. This is the Popovic transcript. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have the transcript before you to see if I'm misquoting you, perhaps. Being a pathologist, in what way -- I'm sorry, I put this question to you: Page 7335, this is the page we're looking at, line 25, you stated that the anthropologists tried to identify individuals by reference to the skeleton. This may have been misinterpreted, but can you tell me, how can one identify an individual by his or her skeleton? Do you mean age, sex, or is there any other way of identifying an individual in this way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: What the anthropologists were doing was to get a sort of general -- basic identification features of male or female, the sex of an individual, and an idea of the age. They could not go any further than that, in terms that they could not say this is such and such a person or not. That was not our role. But what we did do was to take material from each body with a view to perhaps specific identification in the future by DNA analysis. So there were occasional bodies in which we did -- we found documentation in the pockets, but we certainly did not necessarily give that person a specific name. It was just to build up a picture of what type of bodies we had -- we were dealing with, and the specific identification was to be done by other people in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned pockets now. At page 7342, line 25, and at page 7343, line 1, you stated, and I'm quoting: "None of them had any weapons, and only rarely -- and only occasionally did we find some bullets in their pockets." Since your reports do not include all the findings, can you tell us whether the items found in the pockets of the individuals were forwarded for further forensic examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I assume they were. We -- anything found in the pockets was handed to the scenes-of-crime officer, who would deal with it thereafter. Whether it was examined or not, I do not know. We certainly made no specific examination of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of their findings by the scene-of-crime officers, if any, end up in your report? And I mean the findings relating to the contents of the pockets. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Only in very general terms. And I think you will see that in my report I do refer, in general, to things like cigarette lighters, occasional documents, that sort of stuff, but I haven't -- I haven't been specific about it because I didn't think that was the important part, and this -- for my report, anyway. That information is available somewhere, but I have not gone into that in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 7342, lines 2 through 8, you said that in a great many cases, you were not able to ascertain the cause of death and you had to classify them accordingly. In lines 2 through 8, you also said that you could not rule out the possibility that the individuals were members of the army, since they -- most of them were of military age and they could carry weapons and could have been killed in combat. Today, in answer to the Prosecutor's question at page 10 - 21100 [as interpreted], you said that 5 per cent were killed -- could have been killed by a blast, and for a number of them you were unable to ascertain the cause of death. Can you tell me, is the task of a pathologist to ascertain the age of individuals found in the grave or is it the task of an anthropologist? And is it the task of an anthropologist to conclude if the person met his or her death in combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we receive the answer of the witness, could you please check, Mr. Tolimir, if you have given the right page number. It's unclear to me if that is really the part of the transcript in Popovic you were referring to. And Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was my first comment was on line 11 we had -- you said that "in a great many cases." I believe it actually says "in a number of cases" on T-7342, line 6, not "great number of cases." And, secondly, as you mentioned, Mr. Tolimir's reference to lines 2 through 8, I don't believe that's 7342 at all. I'm asking for a transcript reference. And just finally, if we could please break up -- break up the questions there, because I noticed quite a few in that large paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, do you recall anything of the different questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I was going to make the very first point about being misquoted about the "great number." I've said "a number," so it's important to stress that. The last part of the question, perhaps we could deal with that, about the anthropologists. I think I have explained the difference in the roles of anthropologists and pathologists, but we did not work in isolation. We worked together, and the anthropologists gave us information about age range, sex of the body, et cetera, which I incorporated -- we incorporated into our reports, and I think that's only sensible. It brings it all together. We could -- I mean, I'm still a doctor and I can look at a body and I can make my own assessment, but I had expert guidance by the anthropologists. So I think you should picture that the anthropologists and the pathologists work closely together. They fed us information. As I've stressed, it is our job, as a pathologist, to establish cause of death. The anthropologists did not do that. They could offer their advice and expertise, saying that that is a gun-shot injury, or, I suppose, it's not that, but in the end it's the pathologist that decided. And I'm afraid I cannot remember what other parts of the question you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will repeat. Today, at page 21, 10095150 [as interpreted], you said that 5 per cent of individuals were killed in a blast, and in 8 to 9 per cent of the cases, you weren't able to ascertain the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In other words, approximately 14 per cent -- between 13 and 14 per cent, if we add these two cases. Did you list all these cases in your report as "Unascertained"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: There is a 5 per cent of the blast injuries which were -- that was the cause of death, and I think there's a small percentage -- I mean, I could get these figures -- a small percentage who died from a combination of gun-shot and blast. But in the end, I think there's probably maybe, I don't know, 3 to 4 per cent of cases in which we felt unable to give a specific cause of death, and it may well be -- a lot of these cases did still have injuries. It may well be that they still did die of gun-shot injuries, but we felt we had insufficient proof on what we were dealing with. So the vast majority of people did die of gun-shot injuries, or blast injuries, or a combination of both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. What sort of weapon would have caused a blast injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be any explosive device, like a grenade or a rocket. Explosion means that it's something which would -- well, it explodes, it bursts open, and it releases small portions of metal, shell casing, et cetera, and that will damage the body. It tends to cause much greater damage to a greater area of the body because it's a larger -- larger impact. And what we found in these cases was a large area of damage to a limb or part of body, and often with little bits of shrapnel -- of metal from the grenade or the contents of the grenade actually in the body, and that indicated to us that this was a blast injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So in your profession, you'd never describe a gun-shot wound as a blast injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we would distinguish the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. Sorry, Mr. Tolimir. Judge Mindua has a question, a follow-up question to the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, Mr. Tolimir. I would like to just put a follow-up question, following Judge Nyambe's question. When it comes to the injuries that you've described, I would like to know the following. Mr. Clark, on page 22 of the transcript, lines 9 to 11, we saw a skeleton, we saw a skull, and you said that there was a hole that was probably caused by the entrance of a bullet. So there's an entry wound. And I am wondering, would you be able to say which weapon caused this entry wound? You mentioned a bullet, but could it be, for instance, a lance, or can it be something else? Because you are making a difference between injuries caused by a bullet or by an explosion, but in this particular case I would like to know: What is your level of certainty? How could you ascertain that it was, let's say, a bullet in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have P912 back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a very good question, and it gives an opportunity to perhaps explain a bit about gun-shot injuries. This is a skull with a round hole in it, and that tells me that is a gun-shot injury. Now, gun-shot injuries can be caused by different types of weapon. It could be what are traditionally called low-velocity weapons, like handguns, pistols, revolvers. They tend to leave a hole in the skull, but not much in the way of fracturing 'round about. It's just the bullet going through the skull creates a hole and damages the brain and perhaps goes out. When we see a pattern of injury like this in which there's a hole, but a great deal of fragmentation 'round about, that indicates that that bullet has hit that skull with a lot of energy. And when it hits the skull, it loses all that energy, and as a result the skull fragments. And it's a highly typical pattern of what we would call a high-velocity weapon. Now, it has to be said that in a number of cases, we did find bullet holes which were only a hole in the skull and did not have this fracturing 'round about, and we thought, well, that may well be indicative of the use of a handgun, or of a revolver, or a pistol. That may be one possibility. There may be other possibilities, but it is this pattern of fragmentation of the skull which leads us to believe that. Now, the fact that it's a round hole points to this to being a bullet, as opposed to shrapnel. If this was an explosive injury, the -- it would be much more irregular. It wouldn't get this round hole. And the further thing is and you cannot see it on that picture, that when a bullet passes through the skull, it leaves a very characteristic mark. Essentially, the diametre of the hole on the outside of the skull is smaller than the diametre on the inside. So it's like a sort of funnel going in the way. It's called bevelling, it's a very characteristic feature. As I say, you cannot see it there, but we could tell that. That has the benefit of indicating to us the direction of the bullet. That's why we can tell this is an entry wound, as opposed to an exit, because often the bullet will come out the other side. So all of these point to us strongly gun-shot entry wound from a high-velocity weapon. I think you mentioned could this be some rounded, blunt object, some pole, narrow pole. Theoretically, yes, but it would not produce either the bevelling on the inside and it would not produce the surrounding fracturing and the amount of damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your answer was very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to thank Their Honours Judge Nyambe and Judge Mindua for their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question for the witness: It is very important for us to see who was killed in combat and out of combat, and hence my question: Whether a person was killed in combat or in a non-combat situation, is this something that you established solely on the basis of the evidence you found there or was it also based on some independent reasoning of yours? What were the factors based on which you decided whether a person was killed out of combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think I ever took that decision that these people were killed in combat or not killed in combat. I provided information which would perhaps support one argument or the other, and I think there are various groupings of findings to support -- to support one of these. Firstly, if you are thinking of a traditional army in -- men in uniform, with weapons and with bullets, well, none of the bodies we saw had any signs of that. Now, you could argue that after they'd been killed, the bullets and the weapons could have been taken away, and I cannot exclude that in the slightest. You could argue that you don't have to be wearing a military uniform to be a soldier or to fire a weapon. I quite accept that. I can't counter that. So that's one argument. But it has to be said that none of the bodies had any military uniform, and as far as we could see, virtually all of them -- or virtually none of them had any weapons or bullets in their pockets. Secondly, soldiers, by definition, are a generally fairly fit and active population, of fighting age. We were able to establish that in this group of people, particularly from some graves, there was a very wide age range from perhaps teenagers up to people potentially in their 80s or 90s, so not really what you would call a fighting-age population. Additionally, a certain portion -- proportion of these people - I think it's about, in one grave, 4 per cent in the Kozluk grave - had significant disabilities, in the sense of somebody had a glass eye, somebody had had open-heart surgery, somebody had a very rigid elbow, and so they had significant disabilities. Again, hardly a military population. Thirdly, the -- a substantial portion of people in certainly some of the graves, Kozluk, Lazete, particularly, had blindfolds and had ligatures on the wrists, again, which would go against them being traditional soldiers. And I think fourthly, and it's a point that -- it's a more general observation from general reading and knowledge, that typically in a conflict situation between two armies, the majority of people, any deaths are caused by explosion injuries rather than gun-shot injuries, and you could look at any military conflict in history and this would be borne out. And the -- sort of allied to that is that in any traditional conflict, you will find many more people are injured, rather than killed, and to my knowledge -- or at least nobody has ever put that information to me, there were not large numbers of wounded people found in the Srebrenica area. That's for other people to either provide that information or put it to me. So for all these reasons, going from the clothing, the nature of the people, the fact that a number of them had -- were restrained, clearly, and these wider issues, there was very little from the mortuary examinations to indicate that these were conflict/combat casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you've made a number of points now - four that I could count - based on your experience, general knowledge and findings from the graves, and you've just said that this was what you based your findings as to whether a person was killed by a bullet or in some other way, and this is what's important for us: Tell us, please, did you know that individuals -- the individuals in Srebrenica whose mortal remains you examined mostly wore civilian clothes because the area had been demilitarised, and they were not allowed to wear uniforms in public because UNPROFOR would observe that and prevent them from going about their activities? Did anybody tell you this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not specifically. I'm happy to accept that, yes. And as I said earlier, they don't have to be wearing a military uniform to carry a weapon. I'm happy to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in the course of the sanitisation of the general area, that ammunition and materiel and technical equipment was taken away and was not buried together with the mortal remains, and it was taken away by those who buried them? Would this have any bearing on your finding that most of the individuals recovered there were civilians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that information. But I've also -- I think if you go back to my answer, my longish answer, you'll see that I've allowed for that, I've accepted that's a possibility. But I had no specific information about that, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. There is one other matter which would be very important for us to hear your explanation of in order for Their Honours to make their findings. There were witnesses here testifying to the effect that a number of individuals, and in some cases they said more than a hundred, committed suicide. They were part of the column that was trying to break out of the area. Now, what would the chosen criterion be for establishing whether a suicide was committed? They were not in combat with the enemy at the time. They were on their own. We know the specific locations based on witness statements. Would it mean to you, if we told you what the location was, would it have any impact on your subsequent findings as to how the individual was killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's a good point. We made no judgement on any of these deaths, whether this was a suicide, homicide, accident, or whatever. We just provided the information that the majority of people were killed by gun-shot injuries. I have not mentioned anywhere the word "homicide," and certainly not "suicide." I fully accept the possibility of suicide. If you're telling me that -- there are various ways, of course, that you can commit suicide. If you're telling me that they committed suicide by shooting, shooting themselves, then typically people kill themselves by -- when they shoot themselves, by a gun-shot in the mouth or in the head or in the chest. I can't remember of specifically any particular case with that pattern of injury, just a single gun-shot injury perhaps in the mouth. I'd have to look back on all the files. But perhaps you're talking about suicide in other ways, and, in fact, the commonest method of suicide certainly in our country is hanging. And if somebody hanged themselves, that could well be one -- it would leave little, if any, trace at post-mortem. I would not see evidence of that, and that could be amongst the unascertained causes that we saw. So that's a possibility. If they took -- committed suicide by taking an overdose, I'm not going to see that, or certain other ways. Stabbing themselves, I might not see that either. So I think it's a fair point. It would really have to be amongst that small percentage of unascertained cases that they committed suicide. I don't think there's any evidence, in the larger 86 per cent of people or more of the gun-shot injuries, of any typical suicide pattern of that. But other methods, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is the right time for having the first break. We must have our first break now on technical reasons, and we will resume at 11.00. And the Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I would like to mention that the document P16C will be admitted under seal. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like the professor to help us with all his experience, because he sees both one side and another here, whereas we have to rely on his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, would it be fairer, in cases where there are Prosecution witnesses, not Defence witnesses, saying that people killed one another and were not killed in combat, would it be fairer to qualify them as combat casualties, rather than qualifying them as having been killed by shrapnel or gun-shot wounds? Because we did not see the bodies ourselves, so tell us, if there are witnesses saying that over a hundred people were killed in this and that way, and we found a hundred bodies in a meadow killed by grenades or shells, wouldn't it be fairer to treat them as casualties rather than victims of a murder?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I follow -- follow that argument at all. Again, I have not mentioned the word "murder" anywhere in my report. That is for others to judge. I have only said that people were killed in such and such a way, and that could be -- that's not prejudging any situation, whether that's combat, execution, whatever. I'm not actually saying that. I've just given the cause of death and any other information, and it's up to others to take a decision on how and when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. But if there is a witness, a Prosecution witness, not a Defence witness, who claims that in such and such a place, a certain number of people met their death in such and such a way, and another number of people who met their death in another way, is it fairer to place them all in one category as being killed by a blast or gun-shot wound or to say, specifically, that they died in such and such a way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm happy to -- if somebody's put it to me that, These people were killed -- this group of people were killed in this way, are your findings consistent with that, I'm happy to -- yes, yes, I would agree that is a possibility. Somebody else could put to me another scenario, and I could say, well, yes, that's possible, or I think that's unlikely for a number of reasons. But I don't think it's my place to group everybody together and say that they came from -- I have no idea. They didn't come from a particular place. I don't have that knowledge. But I've got my findings, and it's open to either Prosecution or Defence to say, Do your findings fit in with such and such a scenario, and I will say, Yes, or, Perhaps, or, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you a fair question, Professor. We had a Prosecution witness, Jean-Rene Ruez - maybe you heard of him, he was an investigator for a while - and he says that in one location, the so-called location Bare, he found more than 600 victims who were killed by artillery weapons, by shells only. Whether they were killed by direct or indirect shelling, I don't know, but they were killed in combat. And then during the clearing-up of the terrain, they were placed in mass graves, together with other people who were killed by gun-shot wounds, whether from a 10- or 15- or 500-metre distance. How are we supposed to treat them all together as victims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Pardon me. Objection, Your Honours. This misstates the evidence on the record, and if Mr. Tolimir is going to put a fair question to the witness, he should refer him to that piece of evidence so he can comment. My second objection is the witness has said twice that this type of question is outside his role. So, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that was the answer of the witness, but I'm sure the witness is able to answer the question in that way he wants to answer them. Mr. Tolimir, can you give us a reference to the testimony of Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll go on with my questioning while my legal assistant finds the exact reference in Jean-Rene Ruez's testimony, and then I'll put it to the professor. I'm just asking the professor for advice how we should treat these people in this case, because we have different categories of victims, and he has looked at many categories. I'm just putting to him that a Prosecution witness found a certain number of victims killed in this way, and they were later placed in a mass grave. I'm asking how we should treat these victims, as combat casualties or people killed with a specific intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How are we supposed to treat this kind of shrapnel or blast wound? I'm asking you in good faith. I'm not asking you for any answers that would be in violation of your professional ethics. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you want to have an answer, you should be very precise, what you are putting to the witness. Otherwise, an expert witness will not be able to give you a precise answer if you're not able to put the testimony of the other witness in a correct way. I think first you should rephrase the evidence of the other witness, and then you perhaps could expect a precise answer by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but please have understanding for me too. I don't know English, I don't have the transcript, I'm just quoting from memory, and I stand behind what I quoted. My legal assistant will find the reference. I'm just asking the professor, in the context of our discussion, to give us his advice or opinion. If the Prosecution objects to my eliciting such advice, I'll move on, but I believe this is a very experienced expert who can provide us with an adequate answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, I repeat my objection that this misstates the evidence. If we turn to Ruez's testimony on day 16, so the 3rd of May, 2010, 1538, and we have from page -- line, sorry, 16 onwards, and we also have 1537, lines 5 onwards. If you see on page 1538, we're actually talking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Pardon me. If you see on page 1538, we're actually talking about surface remains, not mass graves, so that misstates the evidence. And as again, as Mr. President has asked, I would ask you to please quote the transcript when you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If we could have that part of the transcript on the screen, that would be helpful. Then the witness will be able to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you can just scroll up on 1537 to start off with, you can see the "600," and then again further down on 1538, from line 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1537, lines 5 onwards, and 1538, line 16 onwards, these are the portions Ms. Chittenden indicated that Mr. Tolimir was referring to. Can you see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have nothing on the screen yet. But perhaps I can give a general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps the Court Usher can help you to have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. I think the essential point, he seems to be referring to cases that I had no dealings with whatsoever. Also, the only people that can determine precisely how a person died are the pathologists. The investigators can only give their -- their opinion from what findings they have. And if that coincides with the opinions of the -- in the mortuary, that's fine, but the two may well differ. I'm not sure there's a great deal more I can say. Again, I would reiterate that if it's put to me, from the cases that I have dealt with and my findings, are these consistent with combat casualties, people who have been shot in a combat and then buried, I would say perhaps they are or perhaps they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we scroll up a little bit so that we can see -- no, the other way around. 1538, lines 16 onwards, that was the other portion. Are you able to comment on that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, this is nothing -- nothing to do with me. This is a Finnish team of pathologists, it would appear to be. I have no idea what they found, so I don't think I can comment any further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thank everyone, including Mr. Clark. I think you have managed to assist me in getting an answer that I needed and didn't have, because numbers of such victims do crop up. And I am glad that Ms. Chittenden helped us find the right reference in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, since this was done by a Finnish team of pathologists and they dealt with surface remains, I'm just asking: If such surface remains, about which we have witness testimony that they died in such and such a way, if they are lumped together with all the other victims of the conflict, is that really fair? Should we lump them all together or should we make a distinction based on witness testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That would be fine if we were able to identify which bodies these were, but certainly, in our level of work, we were not able to distinguish that. That might be possible nowadays, with DNA testing, to identify individuals, and then, yes, it might be possible to extract these individuals from the overall grave-site and look at them as a separate group. But we did not have that facility. It might be something that could be done, but that's a fair point. It might be fair to extract that group of people and look at them individually and not lump them in with the others. But I have no way of knowing, at the moment, who was who in a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'll move to another area. I thank you very much, because you shed light on certain facts that I needed elucidated. On page 7343 [Realtime transcript read in error "5343"], lines 10 to 12, you also said, and I quote: "There were a number of those who had physical disabilities that would have prevented them from being involved in combat." Now, my question is: If we proceed from the fact that these are bodies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Just one correction to the transcript. It's page 7343, lines 10 to 12. It's the testimony of this witness in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honour, is under P00892.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Gajic for this reference. I believe the professor has now seen it and I can ask the question, if the professor can see the lines indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you found them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I can't actually see them. But I think it's unlikely that I would have used the word "prevent them from being involved in combat." I would have said it makes it less likely, but I don't think I would have ever have said "prevented them from being combat casualties." Certainly, my evidence this morning was that the fact that a number of people had disabilities would make them less likely to be combat -- a group of combat soldiers. It's not impossible, but it's unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I'm not sure if you have the right part of that testimony on the screen. I don't see anything in the lines 10 to 12 on this page. Now we have another one. We need 7343. Now we have it on the screen. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I accept I have used the word "prevent" there. Well, I mean it in the context that if you have somebody with a very rigid elbow or a rigid knee, it -- well, it certainly would prevent them from being -- using a weapon in the normal sense. So that's -- that's what I mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I understand what you meant. Let me ask you this: Having clarified the previous point, were there many persons with physical disabilities that would have made them unfit to do their compulsory military service, as determined by military medical panels, and were these deformities negligible? I mean, was the number of people with such deformities negligible, because I can't find that in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think it -- Kozluk was an example of -- that was probably the greatest proportion of people who did have significant disabilities. That's -- I think I estimated about 4 per cent had a significant disability. That, of course, is only the disabilities that we could see on a skeletonised body. There may have been others which we could not see. It is fair to say that in other sites, Nova Kasaba, Lazete, Glogova, there appeared to be far fewer people with any significant physical disability and that it was uncommon. Kozluk, it was more common.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, could you tell the Trial Chamber, how do you determine this, because the bodies lay in the grave for a long time, and as they moved from the primary to secondary graves, they sustained further damage? How do you determine such things?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The main disabilities that we could see were disabilities in the skeleton. Now, the skeleton will survive. The tissues of the body will disappear. The skeleton will survive. So if somebody has an abnormal -- abnormality in the joint, for instance, in the elbow, that's still going to be there. It's sort of fused together. Similarly, if somebody has a glass eye, that is still there. Some people did have -- well, had arthritis of the spine, nodules developing in the spine. That is still visible. And one or two -- and those that did have tissues, there was evidence of previous surgery, heart surgery, or metal plates in various places. So evidence did survive in decomposed bodies, particularly when it involved the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would then like to know how we are going to determine heart surgery, previous heart surgery, if the heart is missing, if the tissue is missing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Two things. Sometimes the heart was still present. But in heart surgery, you have to get in to the heart, and we had to do it -- a split down the sternum, so that was still visible, with metal clips -- metal stitches in the breastbone. That was still visible, and that is a very strong indication of somebody who's had open-heart surgery. They split the breastbone, pulls it apart, surgery's done and the breastbone is stitched up with metal stitches, and that's -- they were still visible. So that was the indication. I think there was only one, possibly two, cases who showed signs of that, but they were there. That, of course, is not necessary -- not necessarily a disability, because people have open-heart surgery for a reason and they can recover very well from it, but it was a finding nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. For instance, we had a typical situation, I mean, the cases you worked on, wherein a number of persons you dealt with were killed in the so-called break-out operation in an attempt to cross from one territory to another in a fighting situation, that were trying to break out of encirclement. Could you tell us if there are any typical wounds that would characterise such an attempt to break out from encirclement, and is that a typical military situation that you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, it would be helpful if you could give a reference to the relevant part of the reports of the witness. Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was my objection, or I was going to suggest that he could put it as a hypothetical question to the witness, but not -- if he doesn't have any evidence to refer to there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But as Mr. Tolimir was referring to your reports, you are perhaps able to give us an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't think it's my place to determine what's a military situation and what is not. But to perhaps try and help your answer, a break-out situation would be, I would imagine, people, men, running around and being shot. They could be shot from various directions, perhaps once, perhaps several times. Our findings could certainly fit in with that. But, equally, you could put to me another half-dozen scenarios and I would probably be saying the same thing. But there's certainly nothing that I can say this was highly characteristic of a specific military operation. That's -- there's no way I could say that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Clark. Thank you, Ms. Chittenden, and I apologise for not referencing the transcript, but I just wanted to speak about it in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You spoke of this at page 7360, lines 11 through 15, where you mentioned typical wartime situations, and you spoke of the characteristics of modern warfare. And I was referring to one; namely, a break-out situation. Perhaps you should have a chance to look at this portion of your transcript, rather than me reading it in translation, and perhaps then you can answer my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think I know what you -- what you're referring to. What I was referring to is a paper in the medical literature about in typical combat situations, and I'm thinking large conflicts, that the characteristic injuries of victims are from explosions, rather than bullets, and that more people are wounded, rather than killed. That is looking at a conflict as a whole, perhaps the whole of the Gulf War, Afghanistan, Vietnam, looking at it as a whole.
