Whether that pertains to a very specific incident, which I think you're implying here, a very specific incident, well, it might not apply to the very specific part. All I can say, as a whole, the findings from the mortuary, in terms of the type of injuries found, would point more to a non-typical military conflict. But to get back to your original question about whether the injuries found could be consistent with a break-out, yes, it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have that part of the previous testimony, P892, on the screen. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to everyone, especially to the professor, for not referencing the relevant transcript page in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Can it be established, to a reasonable degree of certainty, the number of victims as a result of a combat in a break-out situation, as opposed to a situation where we have individuals shot before a firing squad or executed in some other way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think I can separate the two very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you tell us, why is it difficult to separate the two? It is very important for us to know in this trial because every added victim incurs a greater degree of responsibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on how you say -- you're putting the scenario of people being -- well, let me start -- in a break-out situation, as you say, I'm imagining that these are men running off somewhere and being fired at perhaps from varying directions, in which case you would expect gun-shot injuries to different parts of the body, different numbers per person. And certainly in a substantial portion of the bodies we saw, that could fit. A firing squad, I think the general picture one would get would be that men standing up, either facing or from behind, and shot once or twice or more times all in the same part of the body or the same surface of the body, then there are cases in these graves which would equally fit with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor, for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness just stopped because you were in discussion with your legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He didn't finish his answer. Please let him continue with his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going on to say that there were a certain number of bodies in which we found only one injury, a single gun-shot injury to the back of the skull or the side of the skull, which could certainly point to an execution or a firing squad-type injury, as opposed to a break-out. That would fit much more with that. One group of -- I can think of one group particularly in the Glogova graves of 12 men tied together, each with a bullet hole in the back or the side of the head, ligatures 'round the wrists. I hardly think that they would be classified under break-out. They're much more likely to be a specific firing squad or whatever. So I think within -- within all our cases, you could find examples of -- which would fit with your scenario of a break-out, some that could fit with the scenario of a firing squad, and some, perhaps, an even closer style -- execution-style killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, and I apologise for interrupting you. I thought you had completed your answer. I wanted you to answer this based on your experience. This is something that you did not explore, yourself, but it's something that we have to deal with. This was an area where there was combat, and both sides are aware of this. And so there was a large number of victims; 2.500 to 3.000, they were all buried in mass graves, and it is common knowledge that they were taken there from an area where there was combat, where there was an attempt to break out to cross over to free territory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I object. That completely misstates the evidence in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you are putting a fact to the witness, you should be precise and give a reference, please. Otherwise, the witness is not in a position to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I understand your position and the position of Ms. Chittenden. I did say that the witness, himself, did not work out in the field, and we have the problem of victims being lumped together into mass graves, regardless of what the cause of their death was. That's why I put this question to him, based on his experience. But I will withdraw the question, if I have to, since I'm unable to reference the transcript page at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not what I -- that was not my guidance. You shouldn't withdraw your question, but rephrase your question. If you are putting to the witness this was an area where there was combat, both sides were aware of this, and so there was a large number of victims, 2.500 to 3.000, if you are putting questions, it is not necessary to have such a statement if you have no reference. So that perhaps you should rephrase your question without such a statement of a fact which we don't know where you did obtain it from. Perhaps you could just rephrase your question and then continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will rephrase my question. I don't know the exact references, and I believe that everyone, including the Prosecution, know that this was fighting that was going on in an attempt to break out of the area. This is something that is known to all the parties. But let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. McCloskey, at the moment Ms. Chittenden is taking this witness, and now after this last -- Mr. Tolimir agreed to rephrase the question. He should do it, and then we receive the answer. Please let him continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: May I speak, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. I think only -- now it is Ms. Chittenden who is taking this witness. It is quite difficult also for the accused to have two counsel responding. Mr. Tolimir, your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Professor, in the course of your work in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, in relation to the autopsies of victims related to the fall of Srebrenica, did you draw upon the services of legal advisors who would, for instance, present you with their theory of what had transpired? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, only in the context of the courts, when various scenarios were put to me, as you are doing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, in answer to the question as to whether your role, as a forensic pathologist, was to dispute any cases or was your role to work toward the verdict of conviction, now, at page 7386, lines 14 to 15, you said: "My role was to collect evidence, and it was up to others to interpret the evidence." Now, at page 7387, lines 15 to 16, you stated: "I wanted to collect information about the individuals as openly and as impartially as possible, and it was up to others to interpret my findings." Does this mean that it was not up to you, as a pathologist, to establish whether a person was killed in combat or was, for instance, shot, executed, and that you should draft your report without presenting any such findings? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, the latter. It was not my role to decide issues -- military -- or specific situations. I've given my findings and again emphasise that nowhere in that will you find that I've said this is definitely combat casualties or this is definitely execution, et cetera. From time to time, I have phrased it in such a way that this would -- the evidence would suggest that, perhaps suggest that or point to that. But, no, it is my role to establish what findings there are, and if that agrees with the proposition put to me by the Prosecution or the Defence, that's fine, but equally it may -- my evidence may go against either of these or not go with it. I'm, if you like, a servant of the Court. I'm not a servant of the Prosecution or the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That's why I was curious about certain points and asked you about it, because I didn't know how to interpret them. I'll move to a different area now, and I thank you for all the answers you've given me in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up P894, please. This is the report by the chief pathologist, entitled -- titled "Srebrenica Grave-Sites." Can we call up -- or, rather, turn to page 2 in both the Serbian and English versions. That's a portion titled "Autopsy Report." We have it on our screens. It reads: "An autopsy report was completed for each body and body part ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Was an autopsy of body parts carried out only once these body parts were associated, and I suppose it was done by the anthropologist, or if not, can you tell us in what way was an autopsy of body parts conducted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We made no attempt to re-associate body parts with bodies. We dealt with the bodies, and then we had a large number of body parts, and we described -- we produced a report for each of the body parts. It was inevitably a much smaller report because we might have been dealing with just a forearm or a hand, so it was a much smaller report, but there was a report for each one. But we made no attempt -- other than, if it was very obvious, we made no attempt to link a body part with a body. That has been done subsequently, nothing to do with me, and all the evidence I'm speaking about in the reports is really to do with the bodies and not the body parts. It's perhaps stretching it to say autopsy report on a body -- on a hand or a forearm. It's a report -- an examination report. "Autopsy" would imply a lot more, but it certainly is an official report on each of the body parts, and that was done without any attempt at association of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Professor. Please tell us, based on what you've just described for us, is it possible to present a higher or a lower number of victims in connection with the body parts that were not linked to a body? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know what you're getting at there. The numbers I have given and are working with are just the whole bodies. The anthropologists, perhaps by looking at the body parts, could indicate that these body -- some of these body parts will be coming from other bodies which we have not seen. For instance, if -- if all 56 bodies in a grave all have a left arm, and we find a body part of a left arm, clearly it's another individual, and by -- that's a simple example. But by such an exercise, it may be possible to say, well, from these body parts, there must be at least another four or five or more individuals represented in that grave-site; the rest of the body, we have not seen. So that is why you may see varying figures. That's -- I have not worked -- my calculations are not worked -- are not based on that. They're based on physical bodies which anybody could count, one, two, three, four. We can see them, and that's what my calculations are done on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Bearing in mind the answer you've just given us, please answer this: In drafting these autopsy reports - I suppose that's what they're called - did both the pathologist and anthropologist write a single report for every body or were these two separate reports that were produced? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It's a fair point. There certainly is a report produced by the pathologists. The anthropologists would have -- they did their own report for each case as well, and from that, from their report, they gave us certain information which we would find useful in our report; for instance, of the age, the sex, and things like that in a body. But as far as I understand it, they have their own separate documentation. I don't know in what format that was produced, whether it was produced into an official report or not, but they certainly had all their own documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. To have a complete answer from you, tell me, does this mean that there would ultimately be the final versions of reports by anthropologists and by pathologists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, there could well be, but we are looking at different things. I think the pathologist's report is what everybody understands as an autopsy report. Description of the body, cause of death, that's a standard autopsy report. The anthropologist will be producing their own report, but entirely for identification, and listing of bones, and aging, et cetera, information. They make no attempt -- as I understand it, they make no attempt to talk about causes of death or interpret all the findings that I've interpreted. I don't know if that helps to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. It is helpful. To have a complete understanding of what you're saying, as a layman, please tell me, did anyone analyse these two reports and draw findings as to the contents of a grave holding 100 to 200 bodies? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: They may well have. I have no idea of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If this was not the case, would these reports then be considered as two separate reports? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: There may well be a report from archaeologists, anthropologists, giving an idea of the overall number of bodies in a grave-site. My report deals with, simply, the whole bodies or virtually the whole bodies that we dealt with, and I'm quite happy to believe that if I'm dealing with 200 bodies from a grave, by other calculations, looking at body parts and other things, there may well have been 230 bodies. I don't know. But I'm -- I'm sticking strictly to the bodies that I can analyse. I would imagine that somebody has looked at these body parts and tried to estimate numbers of individuals, but it's not something that I've been involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In order to fully understand what you've just told us, can you tell us, what were the facts that a pathologist dealt with and what were those that an anthropologist would deal with, as well as an archaeologist, whom you've just introduced, in order for me to be able to understand, whilst looking at reports, which concern what sort of facts and issues? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Probably starting at the archaeologist, the archaeologist is looking at the physical grave, the structure of it and the findings within it, the general findings within it. The anthropologist, as I've explained earlier, is helping -- is assisting both the archaeologist and the pathologist in identifying the individual people and trying to assess how many there are. And the pathologist, at the other end, is -- his main task is -- having been presented with these bodies, is to look at them in detail, list injuries, other findings, and come to a cause of death. Now, the pathologist is the only person who will be looking at the -- or listing the injuries in detail, looking at the clothing, looking at the other findings, and coming to a conclusion about how that person has died. Nobody else has done that. Equally, the pathologist has nothing to do with how a grave is constructed or the other contents in a grave. That's the archaeologist's field. So the anthropologist sort of comes in in the middle there as assisting both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, based on what you just said about the work of the pathologist, the work of the anthropologist, and the work of the archaeologist, I realised that the most meritorious is the report of the anthropologist because they take into account all the aspects of what is found in the graves, in clothes, and the contents of pockets, et cetera. Would it be fair to say that the report of the pathologist is, in fact, the most authoritative, compared to the reports of other experts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, just to correct you, you have said that the work of the anthropologist, they take into account of clothes, the contents of the pockets. They don't. They had nothing to do with that. That, if anything, is the role of the pathologist. Well, I mean, overall, in terms of why people have died, yes, the pathologist's report is the most important, but I'm bound to say that in terms of the circumstances of the deaths and the burial of the bodies, then the archaeologist has the important role there. So we all do have a different role. But if you're looking at you've got somebody who was living and then somebody who's dead, why have they died, the pathologist has the main importance in establishing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That's what I meant. Perhaps I've phrased my question inaccurately. Anyway, I have to work through interpretation. What I meant to say was exactly what you just said. The pathologists are helped by anthropologists and archaeologists in forming their conclusions about the circumstances. Now, as to determining trauma injuries on bodies found in grave-sites, most of the bodies you dealt with were skeletonised. In such cases, would the role of the pathologists be even more prominent, compared to the roles of other experts in these cases, anthropologists and archaeologists?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, first, archaeologists had no -- no role in the mortuary at all, so the archaeologists are not in the mortuary. The only two experts in the mortuary are the pathologist and the anthropologist. You said that most of the bodies were skeletonised. That's not entirely true. Quite a lot did still have some tissue on them, and certainly in some graves. But apart from that, the main evidence of trauma that we had to look at was trauma to the skeleton, to the bones, because the bones remain, tissues disappears. So, really, all our evidence is coming, by and large, from what's on the skeleton. Now, we, as doctors, pathologists, know what a skeleton looks like, in the same way we know what other parts of the body look like. The anthropologist has a specific expertise, just in solely looking at the bones, so naturally they have a lot to contribute to helping us to decide which bone is which, what part of it, if it's in several fragments, trying to link them together. So we really worked together -- closely together, but it's the pathologist that decides, yes, there's an injury to that bone, what does that mean. You don't die from damage to the bone. You die from damage to the tissues 'round about, blood vessels and what have you. So it's really only the pathologists, from their routine practice in their own countries, looking at fresh bodies, can say, well, as you get damage to the bone, it's highly likely you're going to get damage to an organ 'round about, and that's likely to prove fatal. So that was where -- that's where the pathologists differ from the anthropologists. Anthropologists assist us, but we take the final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for clarifying this for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up in e-court pages 6 in English and Serbian of P894. Thank you. It will be easier for me to put my question and for you to answer once we see the document. Now we have it in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "As it was said before, 292 whole or largely complete bodies and 233 body parts were recovered from the grave, the majority from KK3. From anthropological calculations, this constituted a minimum of 340 individuals." I believe you noticed that this concerns the number of bodies. You are here recording an estimate by anthropologists. Does that mean that the minimum number of individuals found in the grave is not your estimate, your calculation; it's something, rather, that you accepted from anthropologists?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: From anthropologists or from archaeologists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What importance is it to the pathologists the number of bodies found in a grave, considering that there are also body parts, as indicated here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, in this grave there were a large number of body parts. We were aware that this was a grave, as I recall, which had been disturbed, and we imagined that most of the body parts were represented, parts of bodies, damaged in removing other bodies from that grave. I mean, you can get a body part for a number of reasons: One, it could be -- could have been separated off in an injury, perhaps in a blast injury, so a foot comes off. That becomes a body part created in life. Secondly, if -- over the years, as bodies decompose and the normal tissues holding parts together, the joints, they will disappear, and so a hand can fall off or an arm can fall off the rest of the skeleton because there's not tissues to join it. Or, thirdly, it could be that the bodies have been disrupted at a later stage after death, perhaps in excavating a grave-site, in robbing, as it's called, removing bodies from it. You can imagine that during an attempt to do that, bodies will be disrupted and we'll be left with parts of bodies, and that is what appeared to be us -- appeared to us to be the explanation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I don't intend to ask anything for pure curiosity. I am asking this because I need it. Since we are dealing with approximately 41 bodies here, a few more or less, do all these body parts that are said to have constituted a minimum of 340 individuals, have they all been subjected to DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just wondering where the reference to 41 bodies came from there. If we could have a reference to that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm quoting from this text on page 6. It deals with the Kozluk grave, and it says, I quote: "As stated previously, a total of 292 whole bodies," 292, I repeat, "and 233 body parts were recovered from the grave, the majority from KK3. From anthropological calculations, this constituted a minimum of 340 individuals." I was looking at a difference between 292 and 340 to see what accounts for the total number shown here in court, and if there are any significant discrepancies we should take into account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think what you're posing, do all the body parts -- do they constitute the missing 42 people -- 48 people, I think. I don't know how much association has gone on since. I would imagine that some of these body parts did come from the 292 bodies, but that was -- that could not be the explanation for all of them, and that a substantial number of the 233 were parts of bodies, the rest of which had been -- was missing. Now, it may be that since then, there has been an attempt to associate these body parts with bodies in other graves, perhaps, but I don't know the results of that. But certainly there are -- there are major parts of bodies missing from this site, that we only -- all we had was some body parts for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you explain, when the number of body parts -- does that imply mutual association of body parts that have not been related to any bodies? Can you explain whether these body parts have been associated with these bodies, or were they lying independently in the grave, quite independently of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I can't answer that with any authority because I didn't see them in the grave. I would imagine that when the bodies were being removed, if this was even -- it was separated from a body but it was obviously linked with it, that would be -- at the time when the body was removed, would be linked in with the body. So, for instance, if you had a man lying face down on the ground, and there was just him, and there was a left arm beside him, he had no left arm, and it was lying right beside the body, I think the decision would have been taken at the grave to include that into him, and that would be a body. So the fact that there are identified body parts would be parts of bodies which those people in the field team really could not associate with any body 'round about, that appeared to be quite separate. Now, where they were, whether they were all in one part of the grave or distributed throughout the whole of the grave, I don't really know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I ask this because it says "body part," and that's not the same as "bodies." I was thinking perhaps they are linked to the bodies or they are entirely separate and have nothing to do -- no features in common with the bodies found in the same grave.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think you can be sure that if, for various reasons, we thought a body part belonged to a particular body, for instance, if it had the same clothing on or it was very -- lying right beside it, or there was some other feature, we would have included that into the body. But the vast majority of body parts, we were not able to associate in the mortuary. We had neither the time nor the facility to try and link them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When you say "body part," do you mean one bone, separate from the other bones in the grave, or do you mean mutually associated bones, a group of bones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Both -- it could have been one single bone, like a femur, but most often it was a small part of a body, like a forearm, a whole arm, or a leg, or a foot. I think if one individual bone was found, a bone from a foot or a hand, they were generally collected all together and dealt with -- dealt with in that way, and there was no attempt -- we didn't really do very much on that. So "body part" means what you and I would imagine it means. It's a part of a body which we can identify as a small part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You see here the subheading "Preservation," the penultimate paragraph in both versions. It says: "The degree of decomposition of the bodies varied greatly, no doubt reflecting their respective position in the grave, the protective effect of adjacent bodies, and how wet or dry that particular area was." And you go on to say: "A substantial number were surprisingly well preserved, with intact leathery skin and recognisable internal organs." Could you explain in more detail this phenomenon wherein different bodies in the same grave are found to be in different degrees of decomposition, and have you come across such cases in other grave-sites, apart from this one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I think if -- in all my work in Bosnia and Croatia and elsewhere, the thing that has surprised me more than anything is the unpredictability of the preservation of bodies in graves. And you're quite right to show surprise that one body in a grave is relatively well preserved and another one is not, it's a lot decomposed. I don't know the complete answer to it, but I can only imagine that it's what we call micro-climate, it's really just what's happening in that particular little area of the grave. It may be that because there's other bodies pressing on it, protecting it. It may be that particular grave is more moist than others, I don't know, or how deep in the grave they are. These are all things which I think we need to look at more. But it was a striking feature that sometimes some bodies were extremely well preserved and others weren't, and this did -- because I've not just worked on Srebrenica sites, but I've seen this in other sites as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you please tell us, in view of this phenomenon: Before your pathological examination of the grave-sites, were there other experts examining the same graves, such as archaeologists and anthropologists, who provided you with information about bodies, about the degree of moisture, and other conditions in the grave? Did you receive such information before you proceeded with your own examination?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Nothing -- nothing official. Perhaps we might have chatted at various stages and both expressed some surprise or observations about these things, but I certainly -- we received no official indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Speaking about this particular case, were there bodies dating back to different periods in the same grave or were they all from approximately the same period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I think it's entirely possible that some bodies could have been in the grave longer than others, it's been added to, but if somebody was to tell me that, no, all the bodies were put in the grave on the same day, I -- I couldn't argue against that either. I mean, one of -- perhaps the other factors about decomposition of a body is how soon after death it goes in the ground, because bodies decompose because of bacteria in the body, and if it's sort of a warm environment or outside, then the body will begin to decompose quite relatively quickly. If the body is buried quickly and then goes into, therefore, a cold environment without any air, then decomposition will be slowed down. So the good preservation of a body may or may not be a factor of having been buried very early -- very shortly after death. That may be a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you tell us, was there any examination done into when the bodies may have been buried, and were there any differences in the time of burial in the same grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm sure there were investigations in that line. I know the archaeologists would be able to tell different times of burial from the construction of the grave and the soil that's been put on it. I just know that from general knowledge and chatting to people. But from a pathologist's point of view, we can't offer any guidance on that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any standard in the pathological -- in the pathologists' profession as to how fast bodies decompose, perhaps based on the calcium content in the bones and other factors that may help determine the age?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the issue about calcium content, but it may well be that that is a factor. I don't think it's the main factor in decomposition. I mean, all bodies will decompose, and we see this regularly in our own practice, decomposed bodies. I know that a body in a warm environment would decompose much more quickly than one in a cold environment. A body in water will decompose in a different way from a body on -- exposed to the air or underground. I mean, there's quite a lot of documentation about that. But I think, equally, there's actually, I think, a lot that we still need to learn, and these cases from these grave-sites have certainly opened my eyes to the variety of changes and the unpredictability of it all. I think we read in the pathology textbooks that you get one particular type of decomposition with a hot environment, one with a dry environment, one in water, and we tend to think they're all separate, but, in fact, you can see all three changes in the one body. That's quite a long answer, and I'm not sure if that -- what the original question was. But decomposition is an area which we're still learning about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That was precisely my question. What is the main criterion for determining the degree of decomposition of a body, as applied in this case? Was it the changes that you discussed in previous answers? What was the reason why these changes occurred faster in some bodies than in others in the same grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We made no real attempt to interpret the decomposition. All I can say is that these bodies were not fresh. The appearances would suggest that they have been dead for at least several months, and very possibly years. Now, I cannot say that they've been dead for three years, four years, or five years. After a while, the changes all merge into each other. But -- so we made really no attempt to specify particularly when these people died.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Can the professor be shown page 7 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next part of this document, perhaps this is the right time for the second break, and you should continue after the break. We will adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question would be: If the witness can recall his previous answer, when we discussed clothing, or perhaps it would be good to look at page 7 of this report. I don't know if you have it in front of you, where it says: "Clothing was still present on nearly all the bodies, some with just a few light items, others with several layers." Layers of clothing, I suppose. Now, my question is: Can you recall if there was some kind of regularity about this, in which part of the grave were the bodies with more clothing and in which part of the grave there were bodies with just a few items of clothing, and is this difference perhaps due to the personal habits of the individuals found in the graves or is it because clothing was removed before the bodies were buried?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I follow your question. I don't -- we made no analysis of that at all. I don't know where a particular body was in the grave. That information will be available somewhere, but it's not something that I've seen or certainly not analysed, so I can't really help you there, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in this issue for practical reasons. For instance, if we have items of clothing which have gunpowder on them, and if the gunpowder found on the clothing is sent for analysis, one can establish the distance from which the individual was fired upon. So I'm asking you, were pieces of clothing sent for further forensic analysis in order to establish the distance from which the individuals found in the graves that you examined were fired upon? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, they weren't. And I think analysis of clothing for gunpowder residue in the situation of a mass grave would be meaningless because of potential transfer from one body to another. It would be one thing to look for that at an individual -- at an individual grave, but in a mass grave would be meaningless. You would perhaps prove gunpowder on a -- on clothing, but it could be argued that came off another body at whatever stage. But certainly we sent no clothing for fire-arms residue. I think, perhaps just to help the Court, what you're probably getting at is that one of the features of trying to identify distance of fire is some of the other things that come out the end of the -- end of the gun, and with -- that means smoke and flame and various other things. And if a person is shot at very close range, then on the body or the clothing, in addition to the hole from the bullet, you will see the smoke and perhaps even flame -- burning which is coming out of the barrel as well. If you go further away, and I mean even just a few feet, then the only thing that strikes the body is the bullet, because the flame and the powder don't travel any distance. They only travel a few inches or, at most, a few feet. So I know what you're trying to get at. If we looked at -- for gunpowder residue, could that -- that might indicate that was at close range, the short answer is, no, we did not look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Was clothing examined in order to establish if these individuals used weapons? For instance, if I was to operate a gun, I would have gunpowder residue on my hands, and there would also be gunpowder residue on my -- on the clothing of the person shot at? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I go back to what I said earlier, that anybody -- just because you fire a gun or you are shot doesn't mean to say there will be gunpowder residue there anyway. There are various conditions that apply. But, certainly, we made no attempt to look for any gunpowder residue on people's hands. I mean, the same argument applies, that it's meaningless in a mass grave, and on somebody -- a body that's decomposed, would be extremely difficult anyway. So we didn't look for it, nor do I think any results we got would be in any way meaningful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Professor, I wasn't referring to body parts, but to pieces of clothing, such as sleeves, for instance, or the pieces of clothing where the entrance or exit hole are located. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've -- that's what I was imagining you were meaning, and I think I've answered that, that in an ideal case, in an individual body, it's certainly something we would look at. But it wasn't done, and it's inappropriate, really, in the situation of a mass grave, unless with very specialised techniques, which we didn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you please tell us, what specialised techniques are these that could possibly be applied in this case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, not really in this case. I'm straying outside my expertise here, but I'm aware that in cases in a normal practice, one can look at tissues, even bone, under a special electro-microscope, and this can detect particles that we wouldn't see maybe in other ways. But I don't know much about that, and it certainly would have been impossible in a situation like this. So, I repeat, it wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Can the professor be shown page 8 in Serbian and English. This is the basis for my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm interested in the distribution of shots. We can see from here that most of the shots were to the trunk, so this is my question: In your experience, would normally, in combat situations, most of the wounds be inflicted in the area of the trunk?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't actually know the figures. I'm not aware of figures from general combat situations. But I would imagine -- the trunk is the largest part of the body, so it's the one that's likely to get the most number of shots. I don't know how that compares in detail with other conflicts, but I wouldn't have thought it differed a huge amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Professor, you obviously stand by what is stated here, so hence my next question. Please look at the last paragraph on page 8 in Serbian, which my assistant tells me is page 9 in English. It's the first paragraph on that page. So I'm interested in the frequency of shots to legs, that particular paragraph. That's the second paragraph on page 9 in English. Thank you. We can see it on our screens, my assistant tells me. I'm interested in the frequency of shots to the legs, which is touched upon here, and those shots being more common than shots to the head: "... it could be argued that a proportion of 27 per cent was no more than might be expected from random distribution, given that the legs account for approximately 36 per cent of the body surface, there must be a possibility that at least some of these injuries represented deliberate disabling shots to the legs, mostly followed by fatal injuries elsewhere, though the latter need not necessarily always have applied." I rushed through it, but I suppose you could read it in English for yourself. This is my question: In the course of examination, were you able to establish the order in which these wounds were inflicted, whether legs were shot first and then next followed something else? Was this something that was based on facts or on the general experience of pathologists? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I can answer that very quickly. I cannot tell that shots to the legs occurred before or after shots elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In relation to what you said here about random distribution, does this mean that it was a random distribution of shots, or was it the result of an intent? I want to have your answer complete on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think, as I've said in the report, that this could just be random shots, and it just happens to be going into the legs rather than the trunk or the arms. But I think why I raised this possibility, there were a number of cases, and I've illustrated one, in which really the only injuries we found were injuries to the legs, and I've illustrated one particular one. It just raised in my mind the possibility of targeting of the legs, but no more than that, really. It's just raising the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for one question, Mr. Tolimir. Is there a possibility to establish if the person who was shot was still standing or lying on the ground when shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the specific details of that, but we could tell if it was -- the shot was going from above, down the top of the foot. I think, from memory, the -- we thought the person was standing or was -- the foot was flat on the ground, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question was not related to this specific case, but in principle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, we can tell -- it's not all that easy with injuries to the feet. With injuries to the skull and some other bones, it is possible to tell the direction of the shot and perhaps the position the person is likely to be in. I think with the feet, it's a lot more difficult, and I couldn't really say with any great degree of certainty whether they were upright or in any other position, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And if you say "feet," you mean also legs, or is it different with the legs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Legs, it's a bit -- it's a little bit more easy to determine direction of shots in the legs. And sometimes we would be in a situation in which we thought a single bullet had caused more than one injury in the leg. Perhaps if the knee was bent, a single bullet could cause an injury to the thigh and to the lower leg, and that might -- that would perhaps indicate the person was sitting on the ground or whatever. I think, generally, it was not all that easy to see what position the person was in when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking that because you were asked by Mr. Tolimir if some of the wounds on the legs were caused by shots before the shots on the chest or after.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question entirely, and I think the answer is it's very difficult to say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order for us to be able to examine a specific situation, can you tell us, is it a typical occurrence that certain -- that incoming shots would hit the chest more often, whereas the outgoing -- or shots to the back would actually hit the legs? So if you had a person running away from you, you would most often shoot him in the leg, whereas if you have a person approaching you, you would rather be targeting the upper part of the body or the head? Is there anything you can tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, there's no way I can read into the mind of people who are shooting. That may be a possibility, but it's not something I can comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My intention was to draw a conclusion from your answer when we have a typical combat situation and a typical non-combat situation. That's why I needed to have your opinion on this. Thank you. Did you draw a conclusion that some of the victims died in what was typically a combat situation, whereas others died in what was typically a non-combat situation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not really, but I'm happy to accept that some of the bodies we found were -- could have been in a combat situation. Equally, as I've already said, there are a number of bodies in these graves which looked far more like specific targeted injuries, the ones with the bullets in the head, maybe a single shot particularly in the head. So I think we've probably got a mixture -- well, potentially a mixture of types of situations in these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Based on what you've just told us, was distance of fire calculated at all in order to arrive at the conclusions you referred to just now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Can we now call up page B [as interpreted] in Serbian, which is page 10 in English, and there we will find a portion of the document titled "Distance of Fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see that the title is "Distance of Firing." I quote: "In the absence of soft tissue on most of the bodies, particularly the skin, it was impossible to say from what distance the shot had been fired; i.e., whether contact, close range or whatever. The only pointer to perhaps some of them being close range was the number of shots neatly placed at the back of the head, either in the midline or behind one or other of the ears." Thank you. I -- yes, I did read "ears." So my question is this: You said a moment ago that it was not possible to establish what the distance of firing was. Can you tell us, what are the elements required for one to establish the distance of fire? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It is, I think I explained earlier, the other features on the body which will come out of the barrel of a gun. And a bullet wound from about a couple of metres, two metres, on a body can look exactly the same as one from 100 metres or 200 metres, and it's really only at the close end that we can get an idea of whether a gun is up against the skin, or very close to it, or just a short distance away. After that, it becomes impossible. In these bodies, these decomposed bodies, there was no way that we could see any burning, staining, soot staining, or any other features around the wounds, so really we read very little into trying to estimate distances. My only -- you are right to point out that little paragraph that I mentioned. Quite clearly, if there is a shot in a series -- a group of cases in which the shot is remarkably similar and remarkably similarly placed, then it's much easier to do that, clearly, from a short distance than from a long way away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you tell us, in this specific case where you worked, how was it established -- how was the distance of firing established, if it was established? Was it based on the entry and exit wound, or was it based on the type of weapon used, or something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already answered and said that we made no -- there was very little we could read into distance of wound, and we really made no interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, in the following paragraph, "Nature of Weapons Used," you say the weapons used were high-velocity rifles: "... this being confirmed by the recovery from many bodies of typical sharp, pointed, copper-jacketed bullets of 7.62 millimetres in diametre." If this kind of weapon was used, high-velocity rifles, does that mean that a close-range shot would pierce the body, including the skull, and is it true that evidence was found that this was possible even at a not-so-close range, from a greater distance, with this type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, with a weapon of this sort, it is quite possible to inflict devastating injuries from quite a distance away. So I'm making no conclusions about how close the weapons were. With high-velocity rifles, that's what they say, the bullet travels at a high velocity, with a lot of energy, and it can be damaging from quite a distance away. It doesn't have to be close up. But the pattern of damage that we saw in the bones clearly indicated that this was a bullet with a lot of energy in it, and it was of the type that would have come from what's called a high-velocity weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let me ask you, as a layman, if a bullet was found in the body, it stayed in the body, does that mean that that person was killed from a higher distance -- from a greater distance, not at close range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's one possibility, not the only one. I mean, when a bullet -- high-velocity bullet strikes a body, it will often -- if it strikes bone, it will be -- it will break up. As well as the bone breaking up, the bullet will break up, and parts of that bullet can leave the body and some parts will stay in the body. If the bullet passes through a body without hitting bone, then it will probably pass right through it and come out the other side undamaged. That's if it doesn't hit bone. So if we have an intact bullet still in the body, then that's slightly unusual because it would indicate, perhaps, that it hasn't -- that it reached the body with a lesser power and didn't lose a lot of energy, and that could be -- for one possibility would be that it was fired from a long distance away, and we're speaking about hundreds of metres away, probably. The second possibility -- well, and so that by the time it reaches the body, it's lost its energy, a lot of its energy. The second possibility is that bullet has been fired from a closer distance, but it has gone through something else beforehand, possibly another body, possibly another part of that person's body, like an arm. So that would be another possibility. And conceivably, in a mass grave, it could have reached there after death, having gone through another body. So the fact that we have intact bullets in a body could mean fire from a distance, but certainly not by any means the only explanation for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I asked you precisely about the cases when the bullet was found in the body, as you stated in your report. You say that in many bodies, bullets were found with sharp, pointed, copper-jacketed bullets of 7.62-millimetre diametre. It's under the heading "Nature of Weapons Used."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: But not all of them intact bullets. These could have been -- that includes bullet fragments, so bullets which have broken up, and we perhaps find the lead core or the copper jacket of a bullet. Sometimes the bullets were remarkably intact. More often than not, there were just fragments of bullets, but it was still possible to -- from the dimension of them, to give an indication of the type of weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. Could we now show page 10 of your report in Serbian and page 11 in English, and I would like to discuss the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My first question -- it's now on the screen. It's paragraph 2 for me and paragraph 1 for you. Did pathologists use a protocol or instructions in order to come up with a uniform, standardised pathologist's report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We used a protocol to record the evidence. When it came to formulating cause of death, different pathologists would have, perhaps, different views. If I can just give an example. If somebody -- if there was a gun-shot injury of the head and perhaps an injury to the pelvis or to the arm, we can be fairly sure that the cause of death was the bullet to the head. That's inevitably fatal. And, personally, I would have given that as a cause of death, gun-shot wound to the head, even though there were other bullet injuries elsewhere. Other pathologists might have included them all, you know, and said gun-shot wounds to the head and the trunk. That's a fair point, but I think overall there's not an issue. The issue was the cause of death was due to gun-shot injury, and that's the important point. I think the specific final cause of death -- this may sound odd, you know, from a pathologist, and the whole point was looking at cause of death, that the actual wording is not all that important. The important thing is that the overall cause of death was gun-shot injury. So that -- and I've tried to explain that a little bit there. I think you would find any pathologist in any country would perhaps take slightly differing views about what they do include in the cause of death and they don't. This was the range of findings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see in this table, under "Unascertained," there were 55 cases of unascertained in this sample?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then if you look below the table, it says: "These figures are a guide, but are open to interpretation. The decision as to what to include in the cause of death was very much a subjective one for each pathologist ..." My question to you is: What do you mean by "subjective" decision by a pathologist? Does that mean that a number of pathologists can come to a number of different conclusions regarding the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I've tried to explain the reasoning there. Some would give the cause which was the inevitably fatal injury. Others would be more inclusive and add, really, all of the injuries there, and that's why they would put: "Multiple gun-shot injuries." That's normal professional practice. I don't think it makes a huge -- a huge issue, because my analysis of -- if you go back to the earlier sections, my analysis of where the injuries hit the body -- struck the body, whether the head or the trunk, is nothing to do with the cause of death. It's an analysis of the injuries themselves. As I stressed, the most important part here is that all but 55 of these people died from a gun-shot injury somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, looking at this page, page 10 in Serbian, page 11 in English, you've just said that out of these 55 cases -- in these 55 cases, it was not possible to determine the cause of death. Now, my question is: When it is impossible to determine the cause of death, like in these 55 cases, is it impossible for a pathologist to decide what the cause of death was and, therefore, impossible to make a reliable conclusion as to the circumstances as to the circumstances in which the person met their death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I think, clearly, if we do not know the cause of death, it becomes very difficult to have any certainty of the circumstances of the death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are at the end of today's hearing. Could you indicate how much time you need tomorrow to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will try to conclude within the first session. If the witness is helpful and gives useful answers and suggestions, then maybe we will go into the second session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You indicated earlier that you would need three to four hours. You should take that into account. Thank you very much again. Sir, we have to adjourn for today, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the same courtroom. Thank you. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
